lessons.title: India VIX: Reading and Trading Volatility Reversion

children.text: India VIX is the NSE's own volatility benchmark, computed from the live bid-ask prices of Nifty index options, and it does one specific job: it converts the entire options market's collective uncertainty about the next 30 days into a single annualized percentage. When India VIX sits near 12 to 13, the market is pricing in a calm month. When it spikes past 25 or 30, as it did around scheduled events and genuine shocks, the market is pricing in real turbulence. Lesson 13 argued volatility reverts more reliably than price. This lesson turns that argument into a specific, tradeable read on India's own volatility gauge.

body.text: India VIX translates the options market's expectation of near-term Nifty volatility into a single annualized number. A spike in India VIX is almost always driven by a specific, identifiable source of uncertainty, and because uncertainty resolves, VIX spikes tend to fade faster and more reliably than most individual stock price moves do.

children.text: Translating a VIX Level into an Expected Move

body.caption: Since VIX is already an annualized figure, dividing by the square root of the number of trading periods in a year converts it into an expected move over a shorter horizon, the reverse of Lesson 13's annualizing formula.

children.text: An India VIX reading of 18 implies the options market expects the Nifty to move, up or down, by roughly 1.1% on a typical day, and by roughly 5.2% over the coming month. That is a genuinely useful, quick mental translation: VIX is not an abstract number, it is a direct statement about how much movement is priced into the next few weeks.
Measuring Stretch Without Assuming a Normal Distribution

markDefs.definition: A measure of where today's value ranks against a historical window, expressed as the percentage of days in that window with a lower value. Unlike a z-score, it makes no assumption about the shape of the underlying distribution.

children.text: Lesson 5's z-score assumes a roughly normal distribution, and Lesson 5 already flagged that real markets have fatter tails than that assumption allows for. India VIX's own distribution is particularly skewed, it sits in a fairly narrow calm range most of the time and occasionally spikes hard, so options desks often prefer a

over a trailing one-year window instead of a z-score. A VIX reading in its 95th percentile over the last year is unusual regardless of what shape the underlying distribution actually takes, which makes percentile rank a useful, distribution-free alternative to the z-score toolkit from Chapter 2 specifically for a variable this skewed.

body.caption: A rolling one-year percentile rank for India VIX, a distribution-free alternative to a z-score.

body.title: India VIX: illustrative behavior around a scheduled event

body.text: This pattern, VIX climbing into a known date and collapsing right after, is sometimes called a "vol crush". It shows up reliably around the Union Budget, RBI monetary policy announcements, and election results, the same 4 June 2024 episode from Lesson 1, precisely because the source of the uncertainty has a known expiry date. Once the announcement happens, the specific unknown that was inflating VIX simply stops existing.

children.text: Not Every VIX Spike Resolves on Schedule

The reliability of a VIX-crush trade depends entirely on whether the uncertainty driving it actually has a foreseeable end. A budget day or an RBI policy date is about as close to a guaranteed resolution as markets offer. A open-ended, ongoing crisis, a global credit crunch like 2008, or a drawn-out geopolitical conflict, has no such fixed expiry, and VIX can stay elevated for months as the underlying uncertainty simply persists. This is the same distinction Chapter 1 drew between a temporary overreaction and a genuine structural break, now applied to volatility itself: an event-driven spike has a reason to be temporary, an open-ended crisis does not.

body.caption: Scheduled event vs open-ended crisis: not the same kind of VIX spike

cells: An ongoing, unresolved situation with no fixed end date
Sharp rise into the date, sharp fall right after
Elevated for an extended, unpredictable stretch
Relatively high, the resolution date is known in advance
Low, there is no equivalent of Chapter 2's half-life to lean on

body.text: Unlike US markets, where VIX futures and options trade directly on an exchange, exposure to India VIX is typically expressed indirectly, most commonly through Nifty options strategies such as short straddles or strangles when volatility is expected to fall, or long premium positions when it is expected to rise. The exact products and rules available change over time and should be confirmed directly with your broker and the NSE before acting on any volatility view. Options strategies carry their own distinct risks, including theta decay and gap risk, well beyond the scope of this lesson.

body.title: Convert VIX into an expected monthly move
body.prompt: India VIX is currently at 22. What is the approximate expected monthly move in the Nifty, in percent, rounded to one decimal place?
body.explanation: 22 / sqrt(12) = 22 / 3.464 = 6.35%, which rounds to 6.4%. A VIX of 22 is well above the 12 to 13 range considered calm, implying the market expects meaningfully more movement over the coming month than usual.

body.title: Which VIX spike is the more reliable reversion trade?
body.question: India VIX spikes from 13 to 24 three trading days before a scheduled RBI monetary policy announcement. In a separate period, India VIX also rises from 13 to 24 over several weeks as an unresolved global banking crisis with no clear end date unfolds. Which spike is the more reliable candidate for a volatility mean reversion trade?
options: Both are equally reliable, since they reached the same VIX level
The RBI policy-driven spike, because the source of uncertainty has a known resolution date
The banking crisis-driven spike, because larger, slower-building moves are always more reliable
Neither is tradeable, since India VIX cannot be traded directly
body.explanation: The RBI policy-driven spike is tied to a specific, dated event, after which the uncertainty is mechanically resolved, closely matching the vol-crush pattern this lesson covers. The banking crisis has no fixed resolution date, so there is no equivalent of a scheduled event to anchor a reversion timeline to, making it a much less reliable setup despite reaching the same VIX level.

cards.definition: The NSE's volatility index, computed from Nifty index options prices, representing the market's annualized expectation of Nifty volatility over the next 30 days.

A distribution-free measure of how stretched a value is, expressed as the percentage of days in a trailing window with a lower value, useful for skewed series like India VIX where a normal-distribution assumption is a poor fit.
A sharp fall in implied volatility immediately after a scheduled event resolves, as the specific uncertainty that inflated it stops existing.
A distinction between a VIX spike tied to a known, dated resolution (reliable reversion) and one driven by an ongoing, unresolved crisis with no fixed end date (unreliable near-term reversion).

points: India VIX converts the options market's expectation of Nifty volatility over the next 30 days into a single annualized number, which can be converted back into an expected daily or monthly move.
Because India VIX's distribution is skewed rather than roughly normal, a percentile rank over a trailing window is often a more honest measure of stretch than a z-score.

VIX spikes tied to a scheduled, dated event, like a Budget, an RBI policy announcement, or an election result, tend to resolve sharply and reliably once the date passes, a pattern sometimes called a vol crush.

VIX spikes driven by an open-ended, unresolved crisis have no equivalent scheduled resolution and can stay elevated for an unpredictable stretch, the volatility-domain version of Chapter 1's structural break.

India VIX exposure is typically taken indirectly through Nifty options strategies rather than a directly traded VIX product, and the exact products available should always be confirmed with your broker and the exchange before trading.
